Before we talk about scans, I'd like to understand what happened and check a few safety questions, because that helps me decide whether a scan is needed and what the best treatment is. Can you tell me in your own words what happened when you lifted, and how the pain started?
reply: It happened on Saturday when I was lifting a big pot plant in the garden, and I felt a twinge right then. When I woke up on Sunday I could barely get out of bed, so it has been about three days now. The pain is low down on the left side of my back, and sometimes it goes into my left buttock. It gets worse when I bend or get out of a chair, and it is definitely worse by the evening, though it feels a bit better when I am lying still with a heat pack. I have worked from home the last two days, mostly lying on the couch with my laptop, and I can walk around slowly.

utterance:
Here's my plan, Daniel. You've done a muscle strain in your lower back — the examination shows a tender, spasming muscle on the left at the base of your spine, with no sign of nerve damage, no signs of infection, and nothing else worrying. This is what we call acute mechanical low back pain, and it's very common after lifting.

About the MRI: I'm not going to refer you for one, and I want to explain why. Scans are not recommended for back pain like yours in the first six weeks unless there are specific warning signs — things like fever, unexplained weight loss, cancer history, numbness in the saddle area, bladder or bowel problems, or leg weakness. You don't have any of those, and your examination is reassuring. Research shows that in cases like yours, an MRI often shows 'wear and tear' changes that are normal for age and don't change treatment — and it can actually make people more anxious and lead to unnecessary procedures. About 9 in 10 people with back pain like this improve significantly within 4 to 6 weeks with simple treatment.

What I've done:
1. Prescribed paracetamol 665 mg modified-release — two tablets every 8 hours, regularly for the next week. Don't take more than 6 tablets a day, and avoid other products containing paracetamol like cold and flu tablets.
2. Prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg — one tablet three times a day with food for 5 days, to settle the inflammation. Stop it if you get stomach pain, indigestion or black stools.
3. Referred you to a physiotherapist, who will give you exercises to get you moving and back to full strength.

Self-care advice:
- Stay active — this is the most important thing. Prolonged bed rest and lying on the couch all day actually slows recovery. Keep gently moving, change position regularly, and go for short slow walks.
- Keep using your heat pack — that's a good strategy.
- When you're back at your desk, take breaks to stand and stretch every 30 to 45 minutes.
- Try to avoid heavy lifting for the next couple of weeks; when you do lift, bend your knees, keep the load close to your body, and avoid twisting.

Safety-netting — please seek urgent care, or call an ambulance, if you develop any of the following: loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in your groin or saddle area, increasing weakness or numbness in your legs, fever with severe back pain, or pain that becomes severe and unrelenting at night.

I'd like to see you again in about two weeks to check your progress — or sooner if things aren't improving. If the pain is still significantly limiting you after 4 to 6 weeks, we can revisit the question of imaging then. Does that all make sense, and do you have any questions?
reply: Are you completely sure I do not need a scan? I am just really worried this is something major.

utterance: I understand — when the pain is this bad, it's natural to worry it's something major. But I am confident: your examination shows a straightforward muscle strain, your nerves are working perfectly, you have none of the warning signs that would make a scan necessary, and your overall health is good. Scanning now would very likely show age-related changes that have nothing to do with this pain, and it wouldn't change what we do — the treatment is the same either way: pain relief, activity, and physiotherapy. The guidelines in Australia and around the world are clear that routine MRI for back pain without red flags does more harm than good. What I can promise is close follow-up: if you're not improving as expected, or if any warning signs appear, we will investigate further at that point. Does that reassure you?
reply: Alright, I understand. I will take the medication and try to keep moving, but I really hope this improves soon.

awards.label: Defensible diagnosis: Mechanical low back pain
